labelPoints.text: The active part is Bacillus thuringiensis spores and their protein toxins. The caterpillar has to eat treated leaves for it to work.
Labels say to treat when larvae are small and newly hatched, and to get good leaf coverage.
Bt strains differ by target: kurstaki products go after caterpillars, aizawai products (like XenTari) cover tougher caterpillar species.

research.text: Bt is alive and it dies. In one soybean leaf study cited by the US National Pesticide Information Center, less than 9% of Bt spores could still grow after 24 hours on the leaf.

source.name: NPIC, Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) General Fact Sheet

research.text: Sunlight itself kills Bt spores: Griego & Spence (1978) measured inactivation of Bt spores by ultraviolet and visible light.

source.name: Griego & Spence 1978, Applied and Environmental Microbiology 35(5)

research.text: Water quality matters for Bt: a 1980 study in the Journal of Economic Entomology looked at how pH affects Bt preparations.

trichoderma.name: Trichoderma bio-fungicide
trichoderma.kind: A living fungus that protects roots
trichoderma.targets: Soil-borne root diseases (Pythium, Rhizoctonia, Fusarium, Sclerotinia)

labelPoints.text: Trianum-P is mixed with water and applied as a drench, through drip irrigation, or by spraying, so the fungus can colonize the roots.
RootShield grows in soils and on roots, shielding them from root-damaging fungi. It is a preventive, not a rescue treatment.
PlantShield HC's label lists Trichoderma harzianum strain T-22 as the active ingredient, the same strain family across several brands.

research.text: Because the product is a living fungus, what it meets in the tank matters: harsh water or incompatible partners can kill it before it reaches the soil. Labels carry storage and compatibility instructions for exactly this reason.

pseudomonas.name: Pseudomonas bio-product
pseudomonas.targets: Fire blight on fruit trees; fungal diseases on leaves, roots and seed

labelPoints.text: BlightBan A506 uses the beneficial bacterium Pseudomonas fluorescens A506 to suppress fire blight on pome fruit and frost damage on several crops.
Howler fungicide's active ingredient is Pseudomonas chlororaphis strain AFS009, used against a wide range of fungal diseases.
Cedomon is a Pseudomonas chlororaphis seed treatment for cereals: the bacteria live on the seed and protect the young plant.

research.text: Like every living spray, these bacteria have to stay alive to work. Storage, water quality and tank partners decide how many are left when the spray lands.

source.name: Howler EVO Fungicide label, Certis Biologicals

beauveria.name: Beauveria bio-insecticide
beauveria.targets: Whiteflies, aphids, thrips, mealybugs, borers and other soft-bodied pests

labelPoints.text: The BotaniGard ES label says it plainly: 'Spores are alive and subject to harm by storage at high temperatures or contact with water for more than 24 hours.'
Same label: 'Do not mix more product than needed for that day. Do not mix product the day before application.' The clock starts when the spores hit water.
Beauveria works by contact: spores attach to the pest, germinate and grow through its shell. The label says control typically takes 7-10 days, so early application matters.

research.text: The same living-spore logic applies to every Beauveria brand on the shelf, whatever the formulation.

labelPoints.text: The virus only works when a caterpillar eats it, so the label demands thorough spray coverage, and several days may pass between spraying and visible control.
Each NPV product matches specific caterpillars: Gemstar LC covers Helicoverpa armigera and tobacco budworm; Spod-X covers beet armyworm.
Labels stress treating young larvae: Spod-X directs use at first and second instar, because larvae must ingest the virus occlusion bodies.

research.text: Indian farmers buy NPV from local producers: Biovirus-H (Helicoverpa) and Biovirus-S (Spodoptera) from Biotech International specify a minimum polyhedral inclusion body (PIB) count per ml.

source.name: Biovirus-H / Biovirus-S product pages, Biotech International

research.text: More registered Indian NPV products exist, such as Helimar (Multiplex, Helicoverpa NPV) and Somstar HA (Agri Life).

bacillus_subtilis.name: Bacillus subtilis spray
bacillus_subtilis.targets: Fungal and bacterial plant diseases, on leaves and in soil

labelPoints.text: Serenade ASO is built on Bacillus subtilis strain QST 713 and the EPA label covers foliar and soil uses across many crops.
Used at planting or through chemigation, the bacteria build a disease-protection zone around the seed or transplant; it is a preventive tool, not a rescue cure.

source.name: Serenade ASO product page, Bayer CropScience US

labelPoints.text: Different strains are different products: QST 713 (Serenade), GB03 (Companion), MBI 600 (Integral). Labels are strain-specific, so evidence for one strain does not automatically cover another.

source.name: Companion label (EPA Reg. 71065-4) and Integral label (EPA Reg. 71840-5)

research.text: The same organism is sold in India, for example Katyayani BAXIL (Bacillus subtilis 2% AS) and IPL Mildown (Bacillus subtilis 2% AS).

source.name: Katyayani BAXIL product page, Katyayani Organics

context.text: Pests destroy 15-25% of India's crops every year, around Rs 1.4 lakh crore, which is why farmers spray at all.

water.text: Water pH changes how sprays perform. UF/IFAS recommends mixing most pesticides at pH 4 to 7 (5.5 to 6.5 is ideal); alkaline water above pH 7 can break down sensitive products in the tank.

source.name: UF/IFAS Extension, Water pH and the Effectiveness of Pesticides (PI193)

jarTest.text: Yara's TankmixIT checks whether products blend physically in a tank - its own terms say the information 'refers only to PHYSICAL TANK MIXABILITY and does not represent a guarantee of chemical and/or biological compatibility.' Whether the living organisms in a biological spray are still alive after mixing is the question bioOasis focuses on.

source.name: Yara TankmixIT, Terms of Use and Disclaimer
